title: Intra-aortic balloon counterpulsation: anatomy, timing, physiology, indications and complications
subject: ss-ctvs
refs: Sabiston Textbook of Surgery 22e Ch 111 (Mechanical Circulatory Support)
Kirklin/Barratt-Boyes Cardiac Surgery 4e Ch 9 (Postoperative Care and Mechanical Support)
AHA/ACC Guideline for the Management of Patients with ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction

steps.say: The intra-aortic balloon catheter enters percutaneously via the common femoral artery. Advance the tip into the descending thoracic aorta, one to two centimetres distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery. Confirming position with fluoroscopy prevents accidental obstruction of the aortic arch branches.
steps.tx: An **intra-aortic balloon pump** catheter is advanced percutaneously through the common femoral artery into the **descending thoracic aorta**. The radiopaque balloon tip must sit 1 to 2 cm distal to the **left subclavian artery** origin. This careful anatomical placement prevents left subclavian occlusion while keeping the balloon positioned safely above the renal artery orifices.

vis.caption: Vascular access and pulse monitoring for arterial catheter positioning. Credit: StewardMD.
vis.alt: Diagram illustrating femoral vascular access and pulse evaluation for arterial cannulation.

steps.say: Inflation begins precisely at the dicrotic notch on the central arterial waveform, which marks aortic valve closure. Rapid helium inflation displaces blood back toward the coronary ostia and forward into systemic beds. This diastolic augmentation significantly enhances coronary artery perfusion pressure during myocardial rest.
steps.tx: Precise timing requires **balloon inflation** to occur sharply at the **dicrotic notch**, which marks aortic valve closure on the arterial pressure trace. Inflation raises diastolic aortic pressure, generating powerful **diastolic augmentation** that elevates coronary and cerebral perfusion during the relaxation phase of the cardiac cycle.

vis.caption: Phonocardiogram and arterial pulse contour showing valve closure timing. Credit: StewardMD.
vis.alt: Arterial pressure tracing illustrating the dicrotic notch and diastolic timing.

steps.say: Deflation triggers right before ventricular systole during isovolumetric contraction. Rapid vacuum emptying of the balloon creates a physiological void that drops end-diastolic aortic pressure. The left ventricle ejects against lower resistance, achieving dramatic afterload reduction and lowering wall stress.
steps.tx: Active **balloon deflation** happens immediately prior to systolic ejection, within the **isovolumetric contraction** phase of the cardiac cycle. This rapid decompression creates a presystolic pressure vacuum that provides substantial **afterload reduction**, shrinking left ventricular end-diastolic pressure, peak systolic pressure, myocardial wall stress, and overall myocardial oxygen consumption.

steps.say: Never insert a balloon pump in significant aortic regurgitation. Diastolic inflation forces blood backward through the incompetent valve directly into the ventricle. The resulting massive ventricular dilatation causes catastrophic pulmonary edema and immediate hemodynamic collapse.
steps.tx: Moderate to severe **aortic regurgitation** is an **absolute contraindication** to balloon counterpulsation. Rapid inflation during diastole magnifies retrograde volume flow across the incompetent aortic valve into the left ventricle, provoking acute **ventricular dilatation**, severe wall tension, and fatal pulmonary edema in unstable patients.

rows: Retrograde flow into left ventricle causes acute dilatation
Pulsatile balloon expansion risks fatal aortic wall rupture
Occlusive disease causes limb ischemia or vessel tear

steps.say: Aortic dissection is another fatal contraindication because balloon action tears the dissected media. Severe peripheral vascular disease also contraindicates femoral insertion. Passing the stiff balloon sheath through tortuous, calcified vessels risks aortic rupture, limb ischemia, and atheroembolism.
steps.tx: Thoracic **aortic dissection** is an absolute contraindication because balloon pulsation can extend the false lumen or cause aortic rupture. Severe **aortoiliac disease** poses high risks of catheter entrapment, arterial thrombosis, and devastating lower **limb ischemia**, warranting alternative temporary mechanical circulatory support options before intervention.

steps.say: The chief clinical indications include cardiogenic shock after acute infarction and mechanical post-infarct lesions. It stabilizes patients with acute ventricular septal defect or ruptured papillary muscle until urgent repair. It also rescues patients who cannot wean from cardiopulmonary bypass.
steps.tx: Key clinical indications include refractory **cardiogenic shock**, acute mechanical complications such as acute **ventricular septal defect**, and acute mitral regurgitation from **papillary muscle rupture**. In each condition, afterload reduction limits left-to-right shunting or regurgitant fraction while simultaneously augmenting coronary perfusion delivery to vulnerable myocardium.

rows: Augments coronary flow and cardiac index
Urgent mitral valve replacement or repair

steps.say: Vascular complications represent the main source of morbidity from balloon counterpulsation. Femoral artery occlusion or thrombosis produces acute limb ischemia with pale, pulseless extremities. Continuous monitoring of distal pedal pulses and compartment pressures detects threatened limbs early.
steps.tx: Lower **limb ischemia** is the commonest major complication, stemming from **femoral artery thrombosis** or large-bore catheter sheath occlusion. Regular assessment of distal **pedal pulses**, motor-sensory function, and compartment tension is mandatory, triggering immediate sheath removal or limb revascularization upon loss of perfusion.

left.title: Limb Perfusion Checks
points: Hourly palpation and Doppler of pedal pulses
Check capillary refill and limb warmth

right.title: Intervention on Ischemia
points: Immediate surgical or bedside catheter removal
Switch to contralateral or axillary support

steps.say: Initiate weaning once inotropic doses drop and hemodynamic stability is established. A cardiac index above 2.2 litres per minute per metre squared allows reduction of the pump assistance ratio. Transition systematically from 1 to 1 down to 1 to 2 and 1 to 3 before catheter removal.
steps.tx: A protocolized **weaning protocol** starts when vasoactive drugs are low and the measured **cardiac index** reliably exceeds 2.2 L/min/m2. The operator lowers the **pump assistance ratio** systematically from 1:1 down to 1:2 and 1:3 over several hours before deflation and sterile removal.

nodes.label: Cardiac index > 2.2 L/min/m2 on low inotropes
Reduce assistance ratio to 1:2 for 2-4 hours
Step down to 1:3 ratio and assess stability
Full deflation, catheter extraction, and groin compression
